decisions.quote: Where Spitzer uses a holistic approach, fundamentally a stylistic analysis guided by the guiding principle of the dampening effect, the present study’s method is based on defining formal patterns to be identified in annotated text to identify instances of relevant stylistic patterns. In the terms proposed by the typology mentioned above, this part of the present study would best be called a re-analysis (of data).
decisions.reason: The study re-analyses the same eleven Racine plays examined by Spitzer (1931) using digital linguistic annotations and formal search queries, making the repetition of Spitzer's study a reproduction (re-analysis of the original texts) supplemented by a comparative baseline.

decisions.quote: Regarding Racine and the Classical Age, it has become apparent that the stylistic patterns identified by Leo Spitzer, and which in the aggregate produce a dampening effect, again according to Spitzer, are even more frequent in Racine’s work than Spitzer showed. In addition, the analysis was able to show that these patterns are present in varying degrees in Racine’s work and in the work of his contemporaries, but without very strong (or statistically significant) differences, for the most part. The dampening effect, if understood as the aggregate use of individual stylistic patterns, is therefore clearly not an authorial signature style, but the mark of an entire literary genre during a certain period, at the very least.
decisions.reason: Because Spitzer's original study was qualitative and non-digital, reproducing original numerical outputs was outside the analysis plan (not checked), while the computational re-analysis and comparative evaluation substantively qualify Spitzer's interpretation of the dampening effect as a distinctive Racinian signature style (robustness challenges).
